description: Malformed frames and the exact error each must produce. Every case here is a deterministic, byte-level input, so both implementations can be checked without a peer. A receiver that parses one of these successfully, or that reports a different code or severity, is non-conformant.

vectors.note: The first four bytes must be ASCII 'DLWP'. Nothing may be parsed before the magic is checked.
A version the receiver does not implement. The receiver must not attempt a best-effort parse (RFC-0001 section 10).
Version 1.0 defines no header extensions, so any header_length other than 24 is rejected. A receiver must not try to skip the extension bytes.
A zero header_length would make the header shorter than its own fixed prefix. Reject before reading the body.
vectors.frame_note: header_length at offset 6 is 0x00, not the 0x18 (24) that an otherwise identical frame would carry. An earlier revision set 0x18, so the frame was byte-for-byte a frame that version 1.0 accepts and the case tested nothing: a receiver following the rules accepted it. A zero header_length makes the header shorter than its own fixed prefix, so the receiver must reject it as ERR_MALFORMED before reading anything that follows the length byte.

vectors.note: A declared body larger than max_frame_bytes must be rejected by reading the header only, without allocating the declared size. 0xFFFFFFFF is the worst case an attacker can request.
vectors.frame_note: Exactly 24 bytes: the fixed header and nothing else, so the body_length field at bytes 20-23 really is 0xFFFFFFFF and there is no body to read. An earlier revision ended one byte short, so the field read 0x000000ff and the trailing three bytes were a body: the frame declared 255 bytes and supplied 3, which a correct receiver answers with wait_for_more rather than ERR_FRAME_TOO_LARGE. The case tested nothing about frame size while appearing to. Being header-only is deliberate too: it is the one case that proves the size check runs before any attempt to read or allocate the body.

vectors.note: The body begins with 0xFF, which is not a valid cbOR initial byte. A receiver must fail the frame rather than pass the bytes through to a per-message parser.
vectors.frame_note: Message type 1 (HELLO) with no flags, and body ff00000000. A body well-formedness case has to be a frame whose body is plaintext cbOR, and an encrypted body is nonce || ciphertext || tag: validating it as cbOR before decrypting would reject every well-formed encrypted frame. HELLO and HELLO_ACK are the only unencrypted types, so the case uses HELLO. An earlier revision used PING and INPUT_TOUCH with no flags set; both must carry ENCRYPTED, so the encryption rule fired first and the frame answered ERR_UNAUTHORIZED, leaving the cbOR rule this case exists to test unreached.

vectors.note: Indefinite-length encodings are forbidden so that a message has exactly one byte encoding (RFC-0001 section 3.2). 0xBF opens an indefinite map.

vectors.note: A value that fits one byte must be encoded in one byte. 0x18 0x05 encodes 5 in two bytes, which is non-canonical.

vectors.note: HELLO must be the first frame of a session. A PING first is a protocol violation, not a warning.

RFC-0001 section 6.2 registers ERR_UNEXPECTED_MESSAGE as fatal, so the session ends. A peer that repeats AUTH has broken the state machine, and continuing would mean guessing which of the two proofs was authoritative.
An unregistered message type is answered with a recoverable error and the session survives, so that a newer peer cannot break an older one by sending a frame it has learned.
A registered message that the negotiated capability set does not include is refused, but the session continues.
An operation on a channel that was never opened is refused. Channel 0 is always open, so the frame must name a non-zero channel.
The agent advertises max_channels; opening one more must be refused without disturbing the existing channels.

A required key is absent, so the message cannot be executed. ERR_MALFORMED is fatal: the body failed validation and the peer cannot be trusted to resynchronise, so the connection closes rather than continuing in an undefined state.

A string where an integer is required is a schema violation, not a coercible input. ERR_MALFORMED is fatal for the same reason as the missing-key case: silent coercion of a coordinate is how a mis-tap bug is born, and continuing after a schema failure leaves both peers disagreeing about the request.
The forward-compatibility rule: an unknown key in a body must be ignored, not rejected. This is the one case where a 'malformed-looking' body is accepted.
Bits 4-7 of the flags byte are reserved. A receiver must ignore them rather than fail, so that the bits can be assigned later without a version bump.
vectors.frame_note: Flags byte 0xF1: every reserved bit set, plus ENCRYPTED, which PING requires. An earlier revision put the 0xF1 in the header_length field and left the flags byte at 0x00: the vector set no reserved bits at all while its name and note said it did, so it passed a receiver that ignored the flag field entirely.

vectors.note: A truncated frame is an I/O error, not a parse error: the receiver must wait for more bytes until the connection closes, then report ERR_IO.

sequence_vectors.note: The sequence number is session-global and must increase. A repeated value is treated as a replay attempt and is fatal, not recoverable.
A gap inside the 32-frame reordering window is legal on a lossy link and must not be reported as a replay.
A frame that falls outside the reordering window is rejected and terminates the session, because accepting it would let an attacker replay very old frames indefinitely.

vectors_note: A frame is a 24-byte fixed header followed by exactly body_length bytes of body, and nothing else (RFC-0001 section 3.1). An earlier revision inserted three bytes between the header and the body of every frame, and added three to body_length to match, so every frame agreed with its own declared length and no length check could detect the defect. Its effect was substantive: the body a receiver decoded began with three bytes of noise rather than with the byte each note named, so the cases named for a leading 0xFF or 0xBF did not exercise that byte at all, and the accepted cases carried a three-byte body that is not a cbOR map. The bytes are not a length or a checksum: reading each note against the decoded body is what identified them. Frames now carry their body immediately after the header.
